title: Integer to Roman
description:
Convert an integer `num` between 1 and 3999 into its Roman numeral.

Roman numerals use `I`=1, `V`=5, `X`=10, `L`=50, `C`=100, `D`=500, `M`=1000, written largest to smallest, except that 4, 9, 40, 90, 400 and 900 are written with a subtractive pair (`IV`, `IX`, `XL`, `XC`, `CD`, `CM`) rather than four repeated symbols. No symbol other than `M` appears more than three times in a row.
hints: This is greedy change-making with a fixed coin set that happens to be canonical.
Treat the six subtractive pairs as extra denominations: 1000, 900, 500, 400, 100, 90, 50, 40, 10, 9, 5, 4, 1.
Repeatedly take the largest denomination that fits, append its symbol, subtract, and move on when it no longer fits.
approach:
**Key insight: once the subtractive pairs are treated as denominations in their own right, the greedy largest-first choice is always correct.** The 13 denominations (1000, 900, 500, 400, 100, 90, 50, 40, 10, 9, 5, 4, 1) are exactly the strings a Roman numeral is built from, and each one can only appear a bounded number of times, so `divmod` per denomination produces the numeral directly.

Why greedy works: each denomination is more than the sum of what can legally follow it (e.g. after taking as many 900s as fit, the remainder is below 900), so no smaller combination can replace a larger symbol. Because `num <= 3999` the loop runs at most 13 iterations and the output is at most 15 characters, so the algorithm is effectively constant time.

A table-driven alternative stores the thousands, hundreds, tens and ones digits as four lookup arrays and concatenates `thousands[num//1000] + hundreds[num%1000//100] + ...`. It is equally valid and some interviewers prefer it.

**Common mistakes:** forgetting the subtractive pairs and emitting `IIII`; iterating the table in increasing order; off-by-one when using `while num >= value` without the `divmod` shortcut.

**Interview follow-ups:** Round-trip test against `roman-to-integer`. Extend beyond 3999 (overline notation or repeated `M`). Discuss why greedy fails for arbitrary coin systems (e.g. coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6) and how this relates to the `coin-change` DP.
